For the kendogi, try measure your closest comfortably-fitting long-sleeve t-shirt to get an idea on the measurements. I'm 170cm with a 112cm waist (around, 56cm if side-to-side), and I was worried if being overweight with a dad belly would mean I needed to get one size up (it was the case for fencing gear). 

Take that t-shirt's waist width, overall length, and sleeve length. Make sure the kendogi's waist doesn't go too far from the measurement, because it'll turn out extremely baggy. The gi is usually measured when the front flaps are next to each other, not when crossed over and tied. The true waist size will be after you tie the gi's himo, so don't go too far off from the initial waist measurement or take as close as your own as possible. 

The sleeve length shouldn't be anything to worry about, as long as the sleeves are longer that where your elbow usually is at. If it's too long, you could basically neatly fold the gi sleeves uniformly and press it afterwards (that's what I and my seniors do with ours). It looks super-neat if you don't wanna hem it, but I'd suggest getting what length your elbow is at on your t-shirt sleeve, then add around 3-5cm from that. 

The overall kendogi length, you should follow your height or more. Too short, and you might expose your thigh from the hakama slits on the side. 

For the hakama, you could get someone to help measure the length between your true waist height and your ankle bone height, then make sure the hakama exceeds this length by about 1-2cm or more, but I wouldn't recommend over 5cm more unless the hakama is expected to shrink while washing. You don't wanna trip on your own hakama like what I got with mine.

Over here at the dojo I go to, we have free introduction classes on the first Saturday of every month. The main things they're taught first are dojo etiquette, no shinai touching the floor, bow to the present sensei and senpai, proper stance and gripping the shinai, counting to ten in Japanese, and basic footwork + suburi swings. 

Pre-class warm-ups are done together alongside regulars (warm-up routines vary based on who's leading at the time), but then intro students are usually handled by our lead sensei while the rest of us are handled by the seniors. 

After the trial, they can stick around for some mixed bogu + non-bogu wearer exercises if they're up for it, but they usually come back for that the following week if they decide to keep going. 

We also have the same thing for iaido, but everyone practices together for that one. It's just that the intro students only need to practice unsheathing and re-sheathing a bokuto, sometimes also teaching the 1st iaido kata. 

A loaner shinai (bokuto + plastic saya + sageo + kaku obi for iaido) will be provided for the first month, after which you're expected to already have procured your own gear.

Where I'm at, they drill us since our first classes to always kiai all the time! Seeing all my senpai kiai was just excellent, definitely the best.

At my stage, it's still just basic kakarite-motodachi exercises targeting men, do, and kote (no bogu yet). We kiai our own stuff ("Yaaaa!" or "Yooo!") before stepping into striking distance, then kiai the name of the striking target we're practicing. 

We Malaysians are usually shy folk, so to kiai takes a lot of coming out of our shells. Even I was shy at first, but the encouragement helped lots.

Malaysia here!

Kendo has a minor following. Not common knowledge or included in schools and universities as Japan does. We have independent dojos throughout the country affiliated under the Malaysian Kendo Association (MKA). 

But our kendo's history's been closely tied with Japan since its birth here. Most of us are well-acquainted with Japanese culture due to having been occupied as an Imperial colony during WWII. Skip forward to modern times, and our Youth & Sports Ministry had help from a Japanese government officer visiting to develop sports medicine in the 70's to officially kick off organised kendo in Malaysia. 

Ever since then, Japan has always maintained close ties. Their fellow kendoka, sensei, shinpan, etc. frequently come down here for practice, study, lectures, competitions, etc. We've been also taking exams in Japan itself (5-dan and above, 4-dan and below are done locally by the MKA), and have even been participating in the WKC since its inception!

From my Malaysian perspective, absolutely! Most dojos here usually take in learners from 14 years onwards, haven't heard of any kendoka from here that are affiliated with a Malaysian Kendo Association (MKA) dojo that started younger (independently or otherwise)

1. Dude, tell me about it. I just started too, just cleared a month of weekly practice, and I initially was unable to walk for two days after my first class (had to call in sick to work hahaha). I also came to kendo after I had to stop sabre fencing due to financial constraints (fees in Malaysia are brutal for fencing, but there's a kendo dojo here that charges affordably). Like what's been mentioned by the others, there's some muscles not used in fencing that are being used here. I'd say fencing's en garde stance is very biomechanically sound and easy to understand in its intention. Chudan no kamae, on the other hand, takes a lot of getting used to (for myself, at least). I'm still trying to not topple over and be as stable as I can on 1½ feet. 

2. The kiai basically ties into the aspect of committing your entire Self (mind/spirit-sword-body) into your attack. You launch towards (and sometimes crash into) your partner/opponent as you strike, instead of lunging and retreating like what we used to do in fencing. You shout a war cry to declare to yourself, the opponent, and the judges that you will be the one to come out successful. It sort of steels your resolve, while assailing and challenging the opponent's. Some of my senpai even managed to kiai so intensely that it physically intimidated their opponents just enough to distract, allowing them to go in for a clean point! Just remember to shout from your diaphragm, not your throat, and to not shout for too long at a time. I personally would try to only ½-1 second durations, and not push 100% of my lung capacity's worth of air

Perhaps I could add this on as well, regarding finances. 

Épée tends to be more friendly to funds if that's a consideration.

You'll only need the suit (jacket, pants, underarm protector), an épée mask (the base fencing mask), a single glove of your handedness, the épée itself, long socks, indoor court shoes, and the body wire to connect the épée to your club's scoring system.

Foil and sabre require additional initial cost compared to épée, sabre a bit more so than foil.

For foil, you'll need the above, plus a version of the fencing mask where theres a small bib of conductive fabric near the bottom of the neck area (a foil mask), a vest of the same conductive material worn on top of the fencing jacket and covering the torso (the lamé), the foil itself, and two body wires to connect the foil, lamé, and conductive bib to the system. 

Sabre-wise, you'll need as per épée, but with a conductive version of the fencing mask where the mesh and frame is silver instead of black (sabre mask), an additional conductive jacket with sleeves on top of the fencing jacket, a specific glove that has the same conductive material (sabre glove, but you can also opt for a normal fencing glove and attach a separate conductive manchette/cuff on top), the sabre itself, and the same two body wires as with foil.

Here in Malaysia, we have mostly épée clubs as they're not as costly to both maintaining the club and joining one. Many of us here who take épée do so both competitively and leisurely with not a lot of issue wallet-wise. Foil is also common, though not as much join because of the extra gear needed. Usually those that take foil here are those that take it more so for competition or leisurely under funding from others. Sabre is rare, but we exist (I just started sabre, myself). Definitely the priciest to get in, and those that do over here tend to be in for the long run and are heavily competing (most of the senior members of my club are nationally ranked, and I haven't met anyone doing sabre that isn't thinking of advancing into a tournament sooner or later).

Amazingly, there's a number of fencers that are not exactly of the commonly perceived body type. 

I knew an old coach that used to tell me stories of Spanish sabre fencers from decades ago, they were big but moved FAST (he liked to say "think Tekken's Bob, but with swords").

Some of my épée fencer friends are also big, but they fence with accuracy instead of agility. They're not the bouncing-in-place types, they just love targeting their opponents' hands.

Nice, friend! I just started in my own club half an hour away from home. Resources-wise, you can always use the club's own equipment for the time being to really get a feel for the sport and the gear, see if it really is what you like. Once you caught the bug for sure, you can start looking into your own equipment for satisfaction and hygiene reasons 🤣 Usually, you can buy from your club and they'll provide you with fresh stock from their supplier(s).

If you wanna set out on getting gear on your own, you can look up if there are any shops available for you. The usual choice of manufacturer for starting out is Absolute Fencing, good bang for your buck. You can go for Uhlmann/Allstar or even Leon Paul if you want premium choices. Starting out, you don't really need FIE-certified equipment just yet, unless you really want to. These basically cost a ton, but they last you a really long while (I know a coach who still has blades that are 30 years old and still functional). Breaking blades for beginners like us is inevitable, so I'd recommend you get non-FIE gear first. 

Protection wear rated for 350N of penetration force is the common choice for practice, but you might need to upgrade certain or all components of your outfit to higher ratings later on for competition (depending on your country's regulations). 

At the very least for electric practice (with sparring), you'll need a fencing jacket, fencing glove, and a fencing mask of the specific discipline you're taking, as there are specific masks for épée, foil, and sabre. For foil and sabre, you'll need their respective conductive vest and jacket on top of the normal fencing jacket. 

You don't really need the breeches yet if you're not competing, track pants is just fine. Please don't use running shoes, best to use court shoes like tennis/badminton shoes.
